1. The vocabularies – the same models under the names of four disciplines
2. Respondents in countries – random intercepts, random slopes, and the evidence behind a slope
3. Individual effects and aggregate associations – composition against context

::: {.todaytake .fs-85}
You leave able to read a multilevel model in the terms of any of the four traditions, to say how much evidence a slope rests on, and to tell an individual effect from an aggregate association
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
Work along in the workspace, on the file of respondents that you built after day 2
:::

::: notes
The second session leaves the country-years for the people inside them. The original author, the OA, tested the claim on individual respondents with a multilevel model, and this session takes that route. We start with vocabulary, because the same models carry different names in sociology, political science, econometrics and psychology, and two of those names mean opposite things in different fields. Then the respondents themselves, on the file that you built yesterday evening from the Eurobarometer files that you downloaded, and we ask how much evidence a slope really rests on when four hundred thousand people share 270 values of unemployment. Then individual effects against aggregate associations, and last the published model, fitted to the respondents. The slides show only the saved outputs of models fitted once to the respondents, because the licence of GESIS keeps the respondents on your own machine.
:::
